2600.name: Atari 2600
2600.description: Originally sold as the Video Computer System, this cartridge console brought Atari arcade games into the home.

32x.name: Sega 32X
32x.description: A cartridge-slot add-on for the Genesis and Mega Drive that added 32-bit processing and ran its own games.

3do.name: 3DO Interactive Multiplayer
3do.description: A CD-based game platform licensed to hardware makers including Panasonic, GoldStar, and Sanyo.

3ds.name: Nintendo 3DS
3ds.description: A dual-screen handheld family that introduced glasses-free 3D and later included the 2D-only Nintendo 2DS.

5200.name: Atari 5200
5200.description: The SuperSystem used hardware adapted from Atari's 8-bit computers and shipped with analog joysticks.

7800.name: Atari 7800
7800.description: The ProSystem played its own arcade-style games and supported most Atari 2600 cartridges.

amiga.name: Amiga
amiga.description: A Commodore computer family with custom graphics and sound chips, with many games distributed on floppy disks.

arcade.name: Arcade
arcade.description: Groups games made for arcade cabinets and dedicated arcade boards from different manufacturers.

atarist.name: Atari ST
atarist.description: A home computer family used for games and music production, with built-in MIDI ports for connecting instruments.

c64.name: Commodore 64
c64.description: An 8-bit home computer with SID sound and games sold on cassette, floppy disk, and cartridge.

cdi.name: Philips CD-i
cdi.description: An interactive compact disc format used by Philips players for games, educational programs, and multimedia.

coleco.name: ColecoVision
coleco.description: A cartridge console whose home version of Donkey Kong helped bring an arcade hit to living rooms.

dc.name: Sega Dreamcast
dc.description: Sega's last home console used GD-ROM discs and included a modem for supported online games.

dos.name: DOS
dos.description: Groups games written for DOS on IBM PCs and compatible computers, including MS-DOS and PC DOS titles.

gb.name: Game Boy
gb.description: The original Game Boy played cartridges on a monochrome screen and could link two handhelds for supported games.

gba.name: Game Boy Advance
gba.description: A Game Boy successor with a wider color screen and its own cartridge format, later sold in SP and Micro designs.

gbc.name: Game Boy Color
gbc.description: A color-screen Game Boy that plays original Game Boy cartridges alongside games designed for its color hardware.

gc.name: Nintendo GameCube
gc.description: A console that uses small optical discs and has four controller ports for local multiplayer.

genesis.name: Sega Genesis
genesis.description: A cartridge console sold in North America as the Genesis and in Japan and Europe as the Mega Drive.

gg.name: Sega Game Gear
gg.description: A handheld with a backlit color screen and a cartridge library that included portable versions of Sega arcade games.

intv.name: Intellivision
intv.description: Mattel's cartridge console used controllers with a directional disc, a numeric keypad, and game-specific keypad overlays.

jaguar.name: Atari Jaguar
jaguar.description: A cartridge console with a numeric keypad on its controller and an optional Jaguar CD attachment for disc games.

lynx.name: Atari Lynx
lynx.description: A color handheld with a backlit screen and a screen-flip mode for left-handed play.

msx.name: MSX
msx.description: A common home-computer standard used by several manufacturers, with games distributed on cartridges, tapes, and disks.

n64.name: Nintendo 64
n64.description: A cartridge console with four controller ports and a controller designed around an analog stick for 3D games.

nds.name: Nintendo DS
nds.description: A dual-screen handheld with a touch-sensitive lower screen and wireless multiplayer in supported games.

neogeo.name: Neo Geo
neogeo.description: The cartridge-based Neo Geo home console, also called AES, brought titles from SNK's MVS arcade library into the home.

neogeocd.name: Neo Geo CD
neogeocd.description: A disc-based Neo Geo home console with CD editions of games from SNK's arcade and cartridge libraries.

nes.name: Nintendo Entertainment System
nes.description: A cartridge-based home console released in Japan as the Family Computer, commonly called the Famicom.

ngp.name: Neo Geo Pocket
ngp.description: SNK's original Neo Geo handheld used a monochrome display and a small set of dedicated cartridges.

ngpc.name: Neo Geo Pocket Color
ngpc.description: SNK's color-screen Neo Geo handheld succeeded the monochrome model and had its own color game library.

ps2.name: PlayStation 2
ps2.description: The second PlayStation used DVD-ROM games, played DVD movies, and supported most original PlayStation games.

ps3.name: PlayStation 3
ps3.description: A PlayStation console that adopted Blu-ray Discs for games and introduced the PlayStation Network.

ps4.name: PlayStation 4
ps4.description: A home console that introduced the DualShock 4 controller and later included Slim and Pro models.

ps5.name: PlayStation 5
ps5.description: A PlayStation generation built around solid-state storage and the DualSense controller, available in disc and digital models.

psp.name: PlayStation Portable
psp.description: The first PlayStation handheld introduced UMD games, and the later PSP go model used downloads exclusively.

psx.name: PlayStation
psx.description: The first PlayStation home console used CD-ROM games and was later available as the compact PS one.

saturn.name: Sega Saturn
saturn.description: A CD-based Sega console with a library spanning 2D arcade ports and early 3D home games.

segacd.name: Sega CD
segacd.description: A disc-drive add-on for the Genesis and Mega Drive, sold as the Mega-CD in Japan and Europe.

sgx.name: PC Engine SuperGrafx
sgx.description: An enhanced PC Engine model that plays regular HuCard games and a small library designed for SuperGrafx hardware.

sms.name: Sega Master System
sms.description: Sega's home console derived from the Mark III, with games released on cartridges and, for some models, Sega Cards.

snes.name: Super Nintendo Entertainment System
snes.description: A cartridge console sold in Japan as the Super Famicom, with games that sometimes used extra chips inside the cartridge.

switch.name: Nintendo Switch
switch.description: A console family built around handheld play, with dockable models that can also play on a television.

tg16.name: TurboGrafx-16
tg16.description: The PC Engine cartridge platform, sold in North America as TurboGrafx-16, used thin cards called HuCards or TurboChips.

tgcd.name: TurboGrafx-CD
tgcd.description: Groups CD games for the PC Engine's CD-ROM² system and its North American counterpart, TurboGrafx-CD.

vb.name: Virtual Boy
vb.description: A tabletop game system with a visor that creates stereoscopic 3D images using red graphics against a black background.

vita.name: PlayStation Vita
vita.description: The PSP's successor added two analog sticks, a front touchscreen, and a rear touch pad.

wii.name: Wii
wii.description: A home console built around the Wii Remote, which uses motion and pointing for supported games.

wiiu.name: Wii U
wiiu.description: The Wii's successor paired the television with a touchscreen GamePad that could display supported games on its own screen.

ws.name: WonderSwan
ws.description: Bandai's original WonderSwan was a monochrome cartridge handheld released in Japan.

wsc.name: WonderSwan Color
wsc.description: A color-screen revision of the WonderSwan that also runs games for the original monochrome handheld.

x360.name: Xbox 360
x360.description: The second Xbox used DVD games and expanded Xbox Live with downloadable titles and a console marketplace.

xbox.name: Xbox
xbox.description: Microsoft's first console used a built-in hard drive and supported network play through Xbox Live.

xone.name: Xbox One
xone.description: The Xbox generation between Xbox 360 and Xbox Series X|S included the original console, Xbox One S, and Xbox One X.

xsx.name: Xbox Series X|S
xsx.description: The Xbox Series consoles share a game library across the higher-performance Series X and the disc-free Series S.

zxs.name: ZX Spectrum
zxs.description: Sinclair's home computer family loaded many games from cassette and included the 48K Spectrum and Spectrum 128 models.
